about.title: A New World Order: The UN, the Cold War and Decolonization
about.length_note: About 30 minutes. There are six topics plus a debate, so each gets a few short steps with a check question. Partition is taken slowly because of the human cost. The frame of reference covers science, politics and people only, because I did not research art or birthdays for this class.

say.text: Welcome to class 56. Today we meet the world that was built after 1945.

show.text: A New World Order: The UN, the Cold War and Decolonization

say.text: We will take it one step at a time: world money, the United Nations, the start of the Cold War, India's Partition, China's revolution, new nations, and a debate about blame.

show.text: 1. World money and the UN; 2. The start of the Cold War; 3. Partition of India and Pakistan; 4. The Chinese Revolution; 5. New nations in Asia, Africa and the Middle East; 6. Debate: who was responsible for the Cold War?

say.text: First, the mood. As World War II ended in 1945, nations were in ruins, and the world wanted peace.

show.text: 1945: ruins, and a wish for peace

say.text: Let's start with money. In July 1944, with the war still on, delegates from 44 nations met at a hotel in Bretton Woods, New Hampshire. It opened only three weeks after the Normandy landings.

show.text: A large resort hotel in the New Hampshire mountains, with delegates from 44 nations gathered outside.

say.text: Why plan money in wartime? They had lived through the Great Depression, and they wanted a better system to rebuild after the war.

show.text: Lesson of the Great Depression

say.text: They created two institutions. The first is the International Monetary Fund, the IMF. It keeps watch on exchange rates and lends to countries struggling to pay for imports.

show.text: IMF: watches exchange rates, short-term loans | World Bank: (coming next)

say.text: The second is the World Bank. Its job was to help pay to rebuild war-ravaged countries, and to help poorer countries grow.

show.text: IMF: watches exchange rates, short-term loans | World Bank: rebuilding after war, and development

ask.q: What was the World Bank's main job in the 1940s?
ask.right: Helping pay to rebuild countries wrecked by the war
wrong: Sending soldiers to keep the peace
Choosing which countries could hold elections
Printing one world currency
ask.why: The World Bank was set up to help finance rebuilding after the war and the development of poorer countries.

say.text: An exchange rate is the price of one country's money in another country's money. Bretton Woods fixed those rates, with the US dollar and gold at the center. That system lasted until 1971.

show.text: Fixed exchange rates: the dollar and gold

ask.q: What was at the center of the Bretton Woods system of fixed exchange rates?
wrong: The British pound and silver
A single coin used by every country
The Soviet ruble and oil
ask.why: The IMF was charged with keeping a system of fixed exchange rates centered on the US dollar and gold.

say.text: From money to peace. The United Nations, or UN, is an organization of countries that was hoped to prevent another world war.

show.text: United Nations

say.text: Representatives of 50 countries met in San Francisco from 25 April to 26 June 1945. They drafted the UN Charter and signed it. The UN officially began on 24 October 1945.

show.text: 25 Apr 1945: San Francisco conference opens | 26 Jun 1945: Charter signed | 24 Oct 1945: UN begins

say.text: There were 51 founding members. Newly independent nations kept joining. Membership reached 127 by 1970, and it is 193 today.

show.text: Number of UN member states

say.text: The most powerful UN body is the Security Council. It has five permanent members: China, France, the Soviet Union, the United Kingdom and the United States.

show.text: Five permanent members of the Security Council

say.text: Each of the five has a veto. That means one permanent member's 'no' can block a major decision. The leaders agreed this at Yalta in early 1945.

show.text: Veto: one 'no' can block a major decision

ask.q: What does a veto on the Security Council mean?
ask.right: A permanent member's 'no' can block a major decision
wrong: A vote to admit a new country
A fine paid by a country that breaks the Charter
A promise to send soldiers
ask.why: At Yalta, each permanent member was given a veto over substantive decisions of the Security Council.

say.text: The UN also wrote down people's rights. On 10 December 1948, in Paris, the General Assembly adopted the Universal Declaration of Human Rights. Eleanor Roosevelt was its driving force.

show.text: Eleanor Roosevelt holding a copy of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights.

say.text: The vote was 48 in favour and none against. Eight members abstained, including the Soviet Union and South Africa. Two were absent.

show.text: How members voted on the Universal Declaration, 10 December 1948

ask.q: Did any country vote against the Universal Declaration of Human Rights?
ask.right: No. Forty-eight voted for it, eight abstained and two were absent
wrong: Yes, the Soviet Union voted against it
Yes, eight countries voted against it
Yes, it passed by a single vote
ask.why: The vote was 48 to none, with eight abstentions, including the Soviet Union, and two members absent.

say.text: Now the Cold War. It was a division of the world into a US-allied half and a Soviet-allied half. They competed for ideological, economic, technological and military supremacy, until the Soviet Union collapsed in 1991.

show.text: Cold War: US-allied vs Soviet-allied, 1940s to 1991

say.text: Tension grew in 1947. President Truman asked Congress for 400 million dollars in emergency aid for Greece and Turkey.

show.text: $400 million for Greece and Turkey, March 1947

say.text: His pledge to help free peoples resist communist expansion became known as the Truman Doctrine. It shaped US foreign policy throughout the Cold War.

show.text: The Truman Doctrine

ask.q: What did the Truman Doctrine promise?
ask.right: US help for free peoples resisting communist expansion
wrong: That the US would give up all its colonies
A new world money system
That the US would never get involved abroad again
ask.why: The pledge to help free peoples resist communist expansion became known as the Truman Doctrine.

say.text: Next came the Marshall Plan. In June 1947, Secretary of State George Marshall proposed big economic help for Europe's devastated nations.

show.text: Not directed 'against any country or doctrine but against hunger, poverty, desperation, and chaos.' (George C. Marshall, June 1947)

say.text: Congress approved it as the European Recovery Program. The plan was open to the Soviet Union and its neighbors, but it stressed free markets.

show.text: Marshall Plan = European Recovery Program

say.text: The Soviet Union refused the aid. It also forbade the communist states of Eastern Europe to accept it.

show.text: Soviet Union said no

ask.right: US economic aid to help rebuild Europe
wrong: A treaty that created the United Nations
A Soviet plan to rebuild Eastern Europe
A system of fixed exchange rates
ask.why: Congress authorized the European Recovery Program, called the Marshall Plan, to rebuild Europe's economies.

say.text: By 1948 the split was sharp. Communists took power in Czechoslovakia. The Soviets sealed off land routes to Berlin, and the West flew in supplies.

show.text: 1948: Czechoslovakia taken over by communists | 1948: Berlin land routes sealed; Western airlift

say.text: Now to South Asia. After the war Britain was weakened and short of money. It left India in 1947.

show.text: Britain leaves India, 1947

say.text: Partition was the division of British India into two independent countries, India and Pakistan. The Indian Independence Act, passed on 18 July 1947, set it up.

show.text: Partition: India and Pakistan

say.text: The two countries came into being in August 1947. Pakistan had two parts, and East Pakistan later became Bangladesh.

show.text: A map of South Asia in 1947 showing India in the middle, West Pakistan to the northwest and East Pakistan to the east, with the lines through Punjab and Bengal.

say.text: The border was drawn in about five weeks by a man named Radcliffe, using outdated maps and census data. It cut through the provinces of Punjab and Bengal.

show.text: A border drawn in five weeks

say.text: About 15 million Hindus, Muslims and Sikhs had to cross the new borders. It was one of the largest human displacements in history.

show.text: About 15 million people on the move

say.text: There was terrible violence. Estimates of deaths range from 200,000 to 2 million. We remember these as real families who lost their homes.

show.text: 200,000 to 2 million deaths (estimates)

ask.q: What was the Partition of India?
ask.right: The 1947 division of British India into India and Pakistan
wrong: The split of China into two countries
The division of Germany into four zones
The founding of the United Nations
ask.why: The Indian Independence Act divided British India into the independent countries of India and Pakistan.

say.text: Mahatma Gandhi, a leader of India's independence movement, was assassinated in New Delhi on 30 January 1948. Many mourned him.

show.text: A crowd in New Delhi mourning Mahatma Gandhi, January 1948.

say.text: Now China. From 1945 to 1949 the Nationalists under Chiang Kai-shek fought the Communists under Mao Zedong in a civil war.

show.text: Nationalists (Kuomintang): Chiang Kai-shek | Communists: Mao Zedong

say.text: The Communists won through military victories and a popular revolution. On 1 October 1949, Mao proclaimed the People's Republic of China, with its capital at Beijing.

show.text: 1945-49: Chinese Civil War | 1 Oct 1949: People's Republic of China proclaimed

say.text: The Soviet Union recognized the new government within days. The Nationalists kept a government on Taiwan, and the US withheld recognition of Beijing.

show.text: Beijing: recognized by the Soviet Union | Taiwan: kept by the Nationalists, backed by the US

say.text: After the Soviet Union, China became the second great communist power of the 1900s.

show.text: Second great communist power

ask.q: When was the People's Republic of China proclaimed?
wrong: 26 June 1945
10 December 1948
ask.why: Mao Zedong proclaimed the People's Republic of China on 1 October 1949.

say.text: Now a big theme. Decolonization is the process by which colonies become independent of the country that ruled them.

show.text: Decolonization

say.text: Why then? European countries lacked the wealth and political support to put down faraway revolts. The US and the Soviet Union both opposed colonialism.

show.text: Europe: poorer and weaker | US and USSR: against colonialism | Nationalist movements: campaigning for independence

say.text: Here are some examples. Korea was freed in 1945 and the Philippines became independent in 1946. Britain left India in 1947. Indonesia won independence in 1949 after a struggle with the Dutch, and the French left Vietnam in 1954.

show.text: 1945: Korea freed | 1946: Philippines | 1947: India | 1949: Indonesia | 1954: French leave Vietnam

say.text: There was no single path. Some independence was peaceful and orderly. In many places it came only after a long, hard struggle.

show.text: Peaceful and orderly | After a protracted revolution

ask.q: Which was NOT a reason empires gave up colonies after 1945?
ask.right: European empires were richer than ever
wrong: European countries lacked wealth and political support
Nationalist movements campaigned for independence
The US and Soviet Union opposed colonialism
ask.why: After the war Europe was weakened and short of wealth, which is why many colonies became independent.

say.text: In the Middle East, Britain left Palestine in 1948. On 14 May 1948, David Ben-Gurion declared the State of Israel. The next day five Arab nations invaded, and the first Arab-Israeli War began.

show.text: 14 May 1948: Israel declared | 15 May 1948: five Arab nations invade

say.text: Now Africa. At the end of 1950, only four African countries were independent: Egypt, Ethiopia, Liberia and South Africa, which was ruled by a white minority.

show.text: Independent African countries, end of 1950

ask.q: How many African countries were independent at the end of 1950?
wrong: Seventeen
Twenty-seven
Forty-eight
ask.why: At the end of 1950 only Egypt, Ethiopia, Liberia and South Africa were independent.

say.text: By the end of 1960 there were 27. Seventeen countries gained independence in 1960 alone, so it is called the Year of Africa. The Congo's independence day was 30 June 1960.

show.text: Independent nations in Africa

say.text: Many of the new nations tried not to be drawn into the Cold War. After the Bandung conference in 1955 they formed the nonaligned movement. Their growing UN membership was the rise in our UN chart.

show.text: Nonaligned movement (after Bandung, 1955)

say.text: Here is a frame of reference. In the same year as the Marshall Plan and Partition, scientists at Bell Labs were building the first working transistor. It was demonstrated in December 1947.

show.text: 17 Nov to 23 Dec 1947: first working transistor built at Bell Labs | 1947: Marshall Plan proposed; Partition of India

say.text: Last, the debate: who was responsible for the Cold War? Historians have argued about this since it began. There are three broad views.

show.text: Orthodox | Revisionist | Post-revisionist

say.text: The orthodox view blames the Soviet Union. It says Stalin broke wartime agreements like Yalta and Potsdam to spread communism. It was the leading explanation until the 1960s.

show.text: Orthodox: the Soviet Union

say.text: Revisionists blame the US more. They say US policy was needlessly harsh and wanted a Europe open to American trade. Some pointed to a push for an 'Open Door' empire.

show.text: Revisionist: more blame on the US

say.text: Post-revisionists say neither side alone was to blame. John Lewis Gaddis wrote the first major account in 1972. Even so, they do not all agree on how to split the blame.

show.text: Post-revisionist: neither side alone

ask.q: What do post-revisionist historians say about the start of the Cold War?
ask.right: Neither the US nor the Soviet Union alone was responsible
wrong: Only the Soviet Union was responsible
Only the US was responsible
Only Britain was responsible
ask.why: Post-revisionists stress that neither the US nor the USSR can be held solely responsible.

say.text: After the Cold War ended, new archives opened. Gaddis then put more weight on Stalin's role. Newer historians look beyond the Washington-Moscow axis to the whole world. So there is no settled answer, and you are free to weigh the evidence.

show.text: No settled answer

say.text: To sum up, after 1945 the UN and Bretton Woods institutions set new rules. The Cold War split the world, Partition and China's revolution reshaped Asia, and many colonies became new nations. Next time: the 1950s and early 1960s.

show.text: UN and Bretton Woods, 1944-45 | Truman Doctrine and Marshall Plan, 1947 | Partition, 1947 | People's Republic of China, 1949 | Year of Africa, 1960

frame_of_reference.elsewhere: The Bretton Woods Conference opened only three weeks after the Allied landings in Normandy, while the war was still being fought.

The UN Charter was signed on 26 June and the UN began on 24 October. Korea was freed by Japan's defeat, and local nationalist movements across Asia campaigned for independence rather than a return to European rule.
The United States granted independence to the Philippines.

Truman asked Congress for aid to Greece and Turkey, and Marshall proposed European recovery aid. British India was partitioned. Bell Labs scientists Bardeen, Brattain and Shockley built the first working transistor, which was demonstrated in December.

Gandhi was assassinated on 30 January. Israel declared independence on 14 May. Communists took power in Czechoslovakia, the Berlin land routes were sealed and the West started an airlift. The Universal Declaration of Human Rights was adopted on 10 December.
The People's Republic of China was proclaimed on 1 October. Indonesia won independence from the Dutch after armed conflict.
Seventeen African countries became independent, and by the end of the year 27 African nations were independent.

other_side.claim: The Soviet Union was mainly responsible for the Cold War (orthodox view).
other_side.other_view: Revisionist historians put more responsibility on the United States, arguing that its policy was needlessly belligerent and aimed at an Europe open to American trade. Post-revisionists say neither side alone was to blame. Later archival work led some historians, such as Gaddis, to focus more on Stalin, and newer historians question whether the story should centre on Washington and Moscow at all.

other_side.claim: Bretton Woods created a fair and shared system for world trade and money.
other_side.other_view: The system placed the US dollar at the center. One historian described it as the start of an 'American economic empire'. The CFR collection, which lists it among the best US foreign policy decisions, links to that view.

other_side.claim: The Partition death toll was about a million.
other_side.other_view: Estimates are disputed. Britannica gives 200,000 to 2 million deaths and about 15 million displaced. Another source estimates up to about 3 million deaths from violence, hunger, suicide and disease, and 14 million uprooted. Historians also disagree about the number displaced and about whether Partition could have been avoided, since some prominent figures opposed it while others favoured separation.
Republicans charged that the Truman administration mishandled China. Britannica instead attributes the Communist victory to military triumphs and a profound, popularly based revolution.

other_side.claim: 1960 was the single moment Africa became free.
other_side.other_view: Historian Katherine Everett argues liberation was more than one moment and should be seen as a process. Counts of 1960 independence also differ slightly (17 in most sources, 16 in one teaching note).
